CausalChain: Chronic liver disease and inflammation lead to altered albumin and bilirubin levels -> these changes are quantified by the ALBI grade, indicating the liver functional reserve -> ICI therapy modulates immune responses in a liver already in a state of inflammation -> immune activation can trigger immune‐mediated hepatotoxicity, causing further alterations in albumin and bilirubin levels -> dynamic changes in ALBI grade during ICI therapy may therefore reflect shifts in the hepatic immune microenvironment -> such changes could predict both treatment efficacy and the risk of liver toxicity.
Hypothesis: Dynamic monitoring of ALBI grade during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy in HCC patients will serve as a real‐time integrated biomarker, predictive of both therapeutic response and the onset of immune‐related hepatotoxicity, as it mirrors concurrent changes in the hepatic immune microenvironment.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treatment has evolved significantly with the incorporation of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Although the albumin‐bilirubin (ALBI) grade has been widely used to assess liver functional reserve, its dynamic changes during immunotherapy may also reflect evolving hepatic immune responses linked to liver toxicity and treatment efficacy. In this context, our hypothesis proposes that monitoring real‐time fluctuations in ALBI grade during ICI treatment may serve as a dual marker: predicting therapeutic response and identifying patients at risk of developing immune‐related hepatotoxicity. This novel approach requires integration of liver function assessment with immunological profiling to better personalize management of HCC patients.
